papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Multilingual Safety in Large Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety assessment of large language models (LLMs) across different languages, highlighting the need for multilingual safety benchmarks. It presents new methodologies for evaluating safety in both English and non-English contexts, revealing that LLMs exhibit higher rates of unsafe responses for non-English queries. The studies propose various approaches to enhance safety alignment and interpretability in LLMs, particularly in the context of Chinese models and specific applications like healthcare diagnostics.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily address safety in a limited number of languages and may not cover all potential safety scenarios. There is also a lack of comprehensive solutions for all types of safety threats, and the effectiveness of proposed methods may vary across different contexts and languages.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies significant gaps in the current understanding of multilingual safety in LLMs, particularly for non-English languages. It underscores the need for further research into safety benchmarks that encompass a wider range of languages and safety issues, which can guide future developments in LLM safety and deployment.

summary: The retrieved literature highlights significant themes in enhancing safety and interpretability of large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts and few-shot recommender systems. Studies emphasize the need for comprehensive safety benchmarks across various languages, revealing higher unsafe response rates for non-English queries, and propose methodologies for improving safety alignment. Additionally, the integration of LLMs in few-shot learning scenarios shows promise for enhancing representation capabilities, although empirical evaluations remain limited. Overall, gaps in multilingual safety assessments and broader applications in healthcare diagnostics are identified as critical areas for future research.
scholarly_positioning: Existing research on large language models (LLMs) has primarily focused on safety assessments in limited multilingual contexts, revealing significant gaps in safety benchmarks for non-English languages and a lack of comprehensive solutions for diverse safety threats. While methodologies have been proposed to enhance safety alignment, they often fail to address the broader implications of interpretability and controllability in LLMs, particularly in high-stakes applications like healthcare diagnostics. Furthermore, the integration of LLMs in few-shot recommender systems has shown potential but lacks rigorous empirical validation, leaving unresolved tensions regarding their effectiveness and generalizability. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing interpretable internal representations that enhance both safety and controllability in LLMs, contributing to a more robust framework for multilingual applications and critical decision-making scenarios.

research_scope: This study will evaluate the safety and interpretability of large language models (LLMs) in the context of healthcare diagnostics, specifically focusing on febrile diseases. The target population will include LLMs trained in both English and Chinese, with a comparative analysis of their performance in multilingual settings. The intervention will involve the implementation of a novel multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) over a six-month evaluation period, assessing the models' responses to diagnostic queries. A control group will consist of traditional diagnostic systems without LLM integration. Primary outcomes will include the rate of unsafe responses and diagnostic accuracy, while secondary outcomes will assess user trust and interpretability of the model outputs through controlled explanation conditions and trust calibration measures.

{
  "Large Language Models (LLMs)": "AI models trained on vast text data to generate human-like text, with a focus on models like GPT-3 and BERT.",
  "Internal Representations": "Hidden states or activations within LLMs that capture semantic and contextual information during processing.",
  "Interpretability": "The degree to which a model's internal workings and outputs can be understood by users, often evaluated through methods like probing and attention visualization.",
  "Safety Outcomes": {
    "Unsafe Response Rate": "The frequency of model outputs that are deemed inappropriate or harmful in a given context.",
    "Over-refusal": "Instances where the model declines to provide an answer unnecessarily, potentially impacting diagnostic accuracy.",
    "Jailbreak Success": "The ability of users to manipulate the model into generating unsafe or unintended outputs.",
    "Harmful Compliance": "The model's tendency to comply with harmful user prompts or queries.",
    "Refusal Precision/Recall": "Metrics assessing the accuracy of the model's refusals in relation to actual harmful queries."
  },
  "User Trust": {
    "Trust Calibration": "The alignment between a user's confidence in the model's outputs and the actual reliability of those outputs.",
    "Blind Trust": "Trust in the model without critical evaluation of its outputs.",
    "Perceived Transparency": "The extent to which users feel they understand how the model arrives at its conclusions.",
    "Appropriate Reliance": "The degree to which users appropriately depend on the model's outputs based on its demonstrated reliability."
  },

    "Probing": "Techniques that analyze internal representations to understand model behavior.",
    "Attribution": "Methods that identify which parts of the input contributed to a specific output.",

    "Attention Visualization": "Techniques that visualize the attention weights of the model to understand focus areas in input data.",
    "Activation Steering": "Manipulating internal activations to influence model outputs in a controlled manner.",

technical_feasibility: The study requires access to open-source LLMs or hidden-state extraction capabilities to analyze internal representations. It also needs labeled datasets for training and evaluation, multilingual prompt sets for both English and Chinese, and native-speaker validation for accurate assessment of model performance. Human participants are necessary for trust calibration measures, which will require ethics approval. Additionally, GPU resources will be essential for running the models, and annotation protocols must be established for multilingual evaluation. If only API models are available, the design should be revised to focus on output-level explanations or black-box evaluations. The study currently lacks access to open-source models and may need to adjust by utilizing available API models with a focus on output analysis instead of internal representation studies.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated the need for comprehensive safety benchmarks in multilingual contexts for large language models (LLMs); however, they treat the effectiveness of safety methodologies across diverse languages as secondary, leaving unclear whether these methodologies can be generalized to enhance safety in non-English applications. This matters practically because higher unsafe response rates in non-English queries could lead to significant risks in real-world applications, particularly in healthcare diagnostics. Therefore, this study investigates the development and implementation of a novel multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) to evaluate LLM performance in both English and Chinese within the defined scope of healthcare diagnostics.
question: How does the implementation of a novel multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) affect the rate of unsafe responses and diagnostic accuracy of large language models (LLMs) trained in English and Chinese when applied to healthcare diagnostics for febrile diseases?
theoretical_mechanism: The proposed research investigates the impact of a novel multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) on the unsafe response rate and diagnostic accuracy of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare diagnostics. The independent variable is the implementation of XSafety, which serves as a mediator through its influence on internal representations and safety detection mechanisms. The dependent variables include the unsafe response rate (system-level outcome) and diagnostic accuracy (system-level outcome). User-level outcomes, such as trust and reliance, are moderated by perceived transparency and calibrated trust, which are influenced by the interpretability of the model's outputs. The theoretical framework posits that enhanced internal representations lead to improved safety mechanisms, thereby reducing unsafe outputs and increasing user trust. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of XSafety in diverse multilingual contexts and the relationship between interpretability and user trust in LLM outputs.
hypothesis: The implementation of the novel multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) will significantly reduce the unsafe response rate of large language models (LLMs) trained in English and Chinese compared to traditional diagnostic systems, thereby enhancing diagnostic accuracy in healthcare diagnostics for febrile diseases.

proposal: This research proposal aims to develop and implement a novel multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) to enhance safety and interpretability in large language models (LLMs) applied to healthcare diagnostics for febrile diseases, specifically targeting LLMs trained in both English and Chinese. Key concepts such as LLMs, internal representations, interpretability, safety outcomes, and user trust will be operationally defined to clarify their implications in multilingual contexts. The study is motivated by the urgent need for comprehensive safety assessments in non-English applications, as existing methodologies inadequately address the higher unsafe response rates observed in non-English queries, particularly in healthcare settings. The literature reveals significant gaps in multilingual safety benchmarks, highlighting that while some safety methodologies have been proposed, they often lack empirical validation across diverse languages and contexts. The central research question is: How does the implementation of XSafety affect the rate of unsafe responses and diagnostic accuracy of LLMs in healthcare diagnostics for febrile diseases? The theoretical mechanism posits that the implementation of XSafety (independent variable) will mediate improvements in internal representations, leading to a reduction in unsafe response rates (system-level outcome) and an increase in diagnostic accuracy (system-level outcome), while user trust is moderated by perceived transparency and trust calibration (user-level outcomes). The falsifiable hypothesis states that the implementation of XSafety will significantly reduce unsafe response rates compared to traditional diagnostic systems, thereby enhancing diagnostic accuracy. Constructs will be operationalized using metrics such as unsafe response rate and diagnostic accuracy measured through response classification and task performance metrics, alongside user trust evaluated via trust calibration surveys. The methodology will employ a benchmark evaluation with a control group of traditional diagnostic systems, ensuring rigorous statistical analyses to compare outcomes while controlling for confounding variables such as model training data variability. Expected contributions include the introduction of the XSafety benchmark, advancements in the analysis of internal representations, and empirical findings on LLM performance across languages, addressing the critical need for safety assessments in multilingual contexts. Key limitations include potential confounding variables, reliance on available models, and challenges in ensuring comprehensive ethical considerations, with a detailed risk analysis to mitigate identified failure modes such as unsafe response generation and over-refusal.

proposal_critique.revision_plan: Revise the gap stage to clarify the specificity and urgency of the identified gap. Strengthen the scholarly positioning by critically comparing methodologies and identifying unresolved tensions. Enhance the clarity of the research scope and operational definitions of key constructs. Provide more detail on the methodology, including statistical analyses and confound control strategies.

rubric_scores.level: 12-13: strong and clear research framing with minor conceptual weaknesses
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal clearly defines the research problem of enhancing safety and interpretability in LLMs within healthcare diagnostics. However, the operational definitions of key concepts like 'internal representations' and 'user trust' could be more precise. Major weaknesses: Some key concepts are not fully operationalized, leading to potential ambiguity in their application. The framing could benefit from a more explicit delineation of the research boundaries. Next band requirements: To move into the next band, the proposal needs to provide clearer operational definitions for all key concepts and explicitly outline the boundaries of the research problem.

rubric_scores.level: 12-13: mostly coherent with minor reasoning gaps
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal presents a logical flow from the identified problem to the hypothesis and methodology. However, some causal claims, particularly regarding the relationship between interpretability and user trust, require stronger empirical justification. Major weaknesses: The assumptions regarding the effectiveness of the XSafety benchmark in diverse multilingual contexts are not sufficiently supported by existing literature. Next band requirements: Strengthening the empirical justification for causal claims and ensuring that all assumptions are backed by scientific literature would enhance coherence.

rubric_scores.level: 15-17: clear novelty with meaningful research differentiation
rubric_scores.justification: The introduction of the XSafety benchmark represents a novel contribution to the field, addressing gaps in multilingual safety assessments for LLMs. The proposal also explores the internal representations of LLMs, which is a less-explored area. Major weaknesses: While the contributions are meaningful, the proposal could further clarify how it advances theoretical understanding beyond existing methodologies. Next band requirements: To reach a higher score, the proposal should explicitly articulate how the contributions extend theoretical frameworks in the field.

The methodology is generally sound, with a clear plan for evaluating the proposed benchmark. However, there are concerns regarding the access to models and the potential limitations of using API models instead of open-source ones. Major weaknesses: The proposal lacks a detailed plan for addressing potential confounding variables and ensuring reproducibility, particularly regarding the evaluation metrics. Next band requirements: Providing a more robust design that addresses confounding variables and ensuring that all methodologies are reproducible would improve the score.

rubric_scores.level: 9-11: relevant literature used but somewhat surface-level
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal engages with relevant literature but lacks depth in critically analyzing competing approaches and identifying unresolved tensions in the field. Major weaknesses: The literature review does not sufficiently position the research within broader debates or explain why existing work is insufficient. Next band requirements: A more thorough critical synthesis of the literature and a clearer identification of research gaps would enhance scholarly positioning.

rubric_scores.level: 7-8: approaching PhD-level with some shallow areas
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal demonstrates some theoretical sophistication but lacks depth in discussing the mechanisms behind the proposed interventions and their broader implications. Major weaknesses: There is insufficient discussion of limitations and potential failure cases, which is crucial for PhD-level work. Next band requirements: Incorporating a more detailed discussion of limitations and failure cases, as well as articulating broader research implications, would elevate the depth.

The proposal is generally well-structured and clear, with a professional tone. However, some sections could benefit from improved conciseness and precision. Major weaknesses: Certain terminologies are used inconsistently, and some sections are overly verbose. Next band requirements: Improving the precision of terminology and enhancing conciseness in writing would strengthen communication.

evaluation.comments: Total score: 74.0/100. Academic level: Master-level. Major strengths: Clear identification of a relevant research problem.; Introduction of a novel benchmark (XSafety) for multilingual safety assessment.; Engagement with relevant literature on LLM safety. Major weaknesses: Insufficient operationalization of key concepts.; Weak empirical justification for causal claims.; Limited depth in literature engagement and theoretical framing. Required improvements for true PhD-level quality: Provide clearer operational definitions for all key concepts.; Strengthen empirical justification for causal claims and assumptions.; Enhance the depth of literature review and theoretical positioning. Final verdict: The proposal demonstrates potential but lacks the rigor and depth expected of genuine PhD-level research maturity.
